titles.secondary: Adrian Mole and The Weapons of Mass Destruction

synopses.short: Adrian goes to Glenn’s passing-out parade. He furnishes his new apartment on credit.
synopses.medium: Adrian goes to Glenn’s passing-out parade. He furnishes his new flat on credit and gets to know Marigold. Read by Harry McEntire.
synopses.long:
The fifth book in the series of readings from Adrian’s diaries, written by Sue Townsend. It starts in 2002 with Adrian aged 34 and covers the controversial period of the Iraq War.

Adrian goes to his son Glenn’s passing-out parade and furnishes his new loft apartment on credit.

His single status is about to change too, putting further strain on his already stretched finances. 

He gets to know Marigold who he met in the bookshop.

As war looms, Adrian is unwavering in his support for Prime Minister Tony Blair and military action, even though his eldest son Glenn is facing deployment to the Gulf.

First published in 1989, Adrian Mole’s diaries were instant bestsellers and Adrian, the remarkably resilient underdog, quickly became a national treasure. While recording the experiences of one individual and showcasing Sue Townsend's fearless and razor sharp wit, the diaries also illustrate how socio-political matters of the time affected the lives of ordinary people.

Copyright Siegfried Sassoon by kind permission of the Estate of George Sassoon

Abridged by Sara Davies.

Read by Harry McEntire.

Producer: Alexa Moore

A Pier Production for BBC Radio 4, first broadcast in April 2019.

titles.primary: All About My Mother: A Memoir of Diana Rigg by Rachael Stirling

synopses.short: Rachael Stirling’s frank, funny and poignant memoir about her mother, actress Diana Rigg.
synopses.medium: Rachael Stirling reads her frank, funny memoir about her mother, the renowned actress Diana Rigg, and the volatile, loving relationship that bound them.
synopses.long:
"What’s it like being Diana Rigg’s daughter?"

For as long as she can remember, Rachael Stirling has been asked that question. 

Legendary actress Diana Rigg was a force – and a mother - to be reckoned with. Her multi-award-winning career took off when she was cast as smart-talking, high-kicking, cat-suited Emma Peel in The Avengers. It was cemented when she played the only Bond girl 007 ever married, and then continued for over 50 years with iconic stage performances in Mother Courage, Jumpers and Medea, and unforgettable TV appearances in Detectorists (in which Rachael played her daughter) and as Lady Tyrell in Game of Thrones.

For Rachael, her mother’s legacy is "a lesson in living life to the fullest: in following your instincts, in taking pleasure wherever there is pleasure to be taken, in loving with all your strength and might, in laughing, always at yourself first, and in being curious, now and forever." Her book reveals her mother as gloriously straight-talking, uncompromisingly frank, fearless and deeply loving. It’s a riotous account of her mother’s life and spectacular career, and a moving testament to the love between mother and daughter.

Rachael Stirling is an acclaimed stage, film and television actress herself, whose appearances include TV’s Tipping the Velvet, Rivals and Detectorists, as well as an episode of Dr Who with her mother.

Episode 5: The Dame, Doctor Who, and a diagnosis.

Abridged by Libby Spurrier

Produced by Sara Davies

Sound design by Matt Bainbridge

Production Co-ordinator: Dawn Williams

A Pier production for BBC Radio 4

synopses.short: Lawyer Gabriel Utterson hears a troubling tale about a man named Hyde...
synopses.long:
Lawyer Gabriel Utterson hears a troubling tale about a man named Hyde. When he discovers that Hyde stands to inherit the fortune of his esteemed friend Dr Jekyll, a mystery begins to take shape. Who is this unsettling stranger, and what hold does he have over the doctor?

Set in the foggy, cobblestone streets of London, lawyer, John Gabriel Utterson investigates the mysterious relationship between his old friend, Dr. Henry Jekyll, and a sinister man named Edward Hyde. What begins as a troubling mystery surrounding a suspicious will, quickly spirals into a dark exploration of science, morality, and the duality of man.

synopses.short: Pearl S Buck's Pulitzer Prize-winning tale of one family's fight for land in rural China.
synopses.medium: Drought and famine drive Wang Lung and his family from their farm. In the city they are reduced to begging and pulling rickshaws, until a workers' riot offers an unexpected chance.
synopses.long:
Written by Pearl S Buck, dramatised by Mary Cooper with MW Sun.

Drought and famine drive Wang Lung and his family from their farm, and in the city they are reduced to begging and pulling rickshaws to survive. A workers' riot offers them an unexpected chance to return home, where, working the land once more, their fortunes steadily rise. But prosperity awakens desires Wang Lung has never had to reckon with, and he becomes consumed by his obsession with a concubine, Lotus.

titles.entity_title: Two Minutes to Midnight by Laura Beatty

synopses.short: Two Minutes to Midnight by Laura Beatty is up for this award for the short story.
synopses.medium: Two Minutes to Midnight by Laura Beatty is the final story in contention for the 2026 BBC National Short Story Award with Cambridge University. Sian Thomas reads.
synopses.long:
‘Two Minutes to Midnight’ by Laura Beatty is the final story in contention for the 2026 BBC National Short Story Award with the University of Cambridge. Sian Thomas reads.

A doctor grieves for her husband and tries to understand the damage being done to the natural world as human intervention continues to threaten catastrophe.

Laura Beatty is the author of two biographies, two novels, two genre-defying books (a mix of travel, history, memoir and fiction) and, recently, two plays. Her first novel, ‘Pollard’ – which the Observer called a “fierce and wonderful” book – won the Authors’ Club First Novel Award as well as being shortlisted for the Ondaatje prize for books which evoke the spirit of place. Her most recent book, ‘Looking for A’, was shortlisted for the Runciman prize. She has also written various short stories, introductions, and reviews. Oxford educated, she began writing in her twenties, while working in the art world in London and New York. She worked for a long time in the voluntary sector, while bringing up children, and then trained to work as a Place2Be counsellor with children up to age 14. Now, she teaches writing both privately and, as a fellow of the Royal Literary Fund, in the NHS and recovery colleges nationwide.

The annual BBC National Short Story Award with the University of Cambridge celebrates its 21st anniversary in 2026 with a shortlist of five short stories by multi-award-winning writers and astonishing new talent from across the United Kingdom. Set in locations across the globe, from the Australian bush to Galway Bay, this year’s tender and vivid stories explore the value of human connection across generations and through friendship in a fractured world. 
Marking the awards is Di Speirs, who has judged the BBC National Short Story Award since its launch. She will be joined on the judging panel by 2022 NSSA winner Saba Sams and two former NSSA shortlistees, Tahmima Anam (2016) and Will Eaves (2017), and Costa Best First Novel Award winner, Andrew Micheal Hurley.  

The BBC National Short Story Award with the University of Cambridge was established to raise the profile of the short form and this year’s all-female shortlist join an impressive list of alumni.

From 14 to 18 September, all five of the shortlisted stories can be heard at 3.30pm each afternoon on Radio 4. The winner of the 21st BBC National Short Story Award with the University of Cambridge will be announced live on BBC Radio 4’s Front Row at 7.15pm on Tuesday 29th September 2026.

Reader: Sian Thomas
Writer: Laura Beatty
Abridged and produced by Elizabeth Allard

synopses.medium: Packed with humanity and humour, Caoilinn Hughes is the fourth story up for this year’s BBC National Short Story Award, which celebrates its 21st anniversary.
synopses.long:
A spectacular encounter in a wintry Galway Bay forces a woman to start imagining a new future for herself. Packed with humanity and humour, Caoilinn Hughes’ story is the fourth contender for this year’s BBC National Short Story Award with the University of Cambridge, and explores grief, female friendship, and things we do in the name of love. Cathy Belton reads ‘A Second Opinion’.

Caoilinn Hughes is an award-winning Irish novelist and short story writer. Her novels include 'The Wild Laughter' (2020), which won the RSL’s Encore Award and 'The Alternatives' (2024). Her short stories have won the Irish Book Awards’ Story of the Year, the Moth Short Story Prize, and an O. Henry Prize. Her story, ‘Two Hands’, was shortlisted for the BBC National Short Story Award, 2025. Caoilinn Hughes grew up in Galway and now lives in London.

Listen to Sherlock Holmes Short Stories, narrated by Hugh Bonneville.

A woman struck dead after hearing a haunting whistle. A series of child-like drawings scrawled throughout a country estate. A prize horse wandering the moors without an owner.

To the regular observer, these are merely strange anomalies. But for the master detective Sherlock Holmes they are the first pieces of an elaborate puzzle.

New episodes every Thursday.

synopses.short: Cherise Saywell’s ‘Ditto’ is up for the prestigious 2026 BBC National Short Story Award.
synopses.medium: Set in a small town in rural Australia, Cherise Saywell’s ‘Ditto’ is the third story up for the BBC National Short Story Award with the University of Cambridge. Richard Goulding reads.
synopses.long:
Cherise Saywell’s story ‘Ditto’ transports us to a small town in 1990s rural Australia in the third of our shortlisted stories in contention of the 2026 BBC National Short Story Award with the University of Cambridge.

In this delicately crafted story, we follow our young narrator as he faces indecision and uncertainty, building up the courage to make a very important phone call. Richard Goulding reads this dark tale which, ultimately, has hope and salvation at its heart.

Cherise Saywell is a novelist and short-story writer. She was born and brought up in Australia and, after travelling to the UK in 1996, has lived in Scotland ever since. The author of two novels, 'Desert Fish' (2011) and 'Twitcher' (2013), her short stories have been anthologised and won the Pindrop Short Story Award (2016), the Mslexia Short Story Prize (2015), and the V.S. Pritchett prize (2003), as well as being shortlisted for several prizes, including the Bristol Prize and the Asham Award. Cherise has been a Royal Literary Fund (RLF) Fellow at Stirling University and Strathclyde University. She now works on the RLF’s Bridge project in secondary schools, and as an RLF Consultant in universities. Born and raised in Australia, Cherise now lives in Edinburgh, Scotland. 

The annual BBC National Short Story Award with the University of Cambridge celebrates its 21st anniversary in 2026 with a shortlist of five short stories by multi-award-winning writers and astonishing new talent from across the United Kingdom. Set in locations across the globe, from the Australian bush to Galway Bay, this year’s tender and vivid stories explore the value of human connection across generations and through friendship in a fractured world. 
Marking the awards is Di Speirs, who has judged the BBC National Short Story Award since its launch. She will be joined on the judging panel by 2022 NSSA winner Saba Sams and two former NSSA shortlistees, Tahmima Anam (2016) and Will Eaves (2017), and Costa Best First Novel Award winner, Andrew Micheal Hurley.  

The BBC National Short Story Award with the University of Cambridge was established to raise the profile of the short form and this year’s all-female shortlist join an impressive list of alumni.

From 14 to 18 September, all five of the shortlisted stories can be heard at 3.30pm each afternoon on Radio 4. The winner of the 21st BBC National Short Story Award with the University of Cambridge will be announced live on BBC Radio 4’s Front Row at 7.15pm on Tuesday 29 September 2026.

Reader: Richard Goulding
Writer: Cherise Saywell
Abridged by Elizabeth Allard
Produced by Bethany Woodhead

synopses.long:
Read by Anne-Marie Duff, ‘Little Lands’ by Lucy Caldwell is the second story up for this year's BBC National Short Story Award with the University of Cambridge in its 21st year.
This beautifully written story centres on a single scene from one of cinema's most iconic films. Reflecting on the famous dance scene in 'The Sound of Music', this story is a meditation on how the sharing of everyday pleasures can be transformed into precious memories to be recalled and passed on.
Lucy Caldwell was born in Belfast and is the author of four novels, several stage plays and radio dramas, and four collections of short stories: 'Multitudes', 'Intimacies', 'Openings', and most recently, 'Devotions'. Elected a Fellow of the Royal Society of Literature in 2018, she was the editor of 'Being Various: New Irish Short Stories' in 2019. She won the BBC National Short Story Award in 2021 for ‘All the People Were Mean and Bad’. Other awards include the Rooney Prize for Irish Literature, the George Devine Award, the Dylan Thomas Prize, the Walter Scott Prize, and the 2022 E. M. Forster Award from the American Academy of Arts & Letters. She runs a popular online masterclass on the short story for the Faber Academy.

synopses.short: The first contender for this year’s BBC National Short Story Award by Merryn Glover.
synopses.medium: Merryn Glover’s heart-rending story set in the Australian bush is the first contender for the 2026 BBC National Short Story Award, which celebrates its 21st anniversary this year.
synopses.long:
Merryn Glover’s heart-rending story about sorrow, love and belonging set in the Australian bush is the first contender for this year’s BBC National Short Story Award with the University of Cambridge, which celebrates its 21st anniversary this year. When an unexpected letter arrives, an elderly man is forced to question his isolated life, surrounded only by animals, birds, and painful memories. Mike Sengelow reads ‘Burning Bush’.

Merryn Glover was born in Nepal, educated in Australia. Her plays and short stories have been broadcast on BBC Radio 4 and Radio Scotland and widely anthologised. Her first novel, 'A House Called Askival' (2014) is set in an Indian hill-station, where she went to school, and her second, 'Of Stone and Sky' (2021), in the Badenoch region of the Cairngorms National Park, is where she now lives. It won Book of the Year at the Bookmark Book Festival, Blairgowrie, and was long-listed for the Highland Book Prize. In 2019, Merryn was the first Writer in Residence for the Cairngorms National Park and has been a regular contributor to the Guardian Country Diary. Her latest book is 'The Hidden Fires: A Cairngorms Journey with Nan Shepherd' (2023).

synopses.short: In Ben Macintyre's new book his Cold War story of espionage in 1980s Iran concludes.
synopses.medium: Ben Macintyre's latest book tells a story of Cold War espionage set against the backdrop of Iran's revolution in the 1980s. Today, there is a reckoning. Read by Jamie Parker.
synopses.long:
Ben Macintyre's latest book tells a story of Cold War espionage set against the backdrop of Iran's revolution in the 1980s. Today, there is a reckoning. Read by Jamie Parker.

The best-selling historian Ben Macintyre's new book is a timely and remarkable story.

It's 1981, Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini has swept to power and the Soviets are preparing to overthrow his fledgling Islamist regime. If their plans were to succeed, the American response could see the Western superpower resort to nuclear weapons. One double agent sets out to thwart the KGB and change the course of the Cold War. In turning to the MI6, the Soviet spy set in train a series of events that continue to have ramifications in the Middle-East and throughout the world today.

Ben Macintyre is the acclaimed author of many best-selling books including several titles which have featured as Book of the Weeks on BBC Radio 4. They include The Siege, Colditz, The Spy and the Traitor and Operation Mincemeat. Many of his books have been adapted for stage and screen. Series three of SAS: Rogue Heroes is in production, and The Siege is being adapted for the screen.  Ben Macintyre is a columnist and Associate Editor at The Times.

Jamie Parker is an award-winning English actor and singer known for originating the role of Harry Potter in the West End and Broadway productions of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child. He won the 2017 Laurence Olivier Award for Best Actor and received a Tony Award nomination. He also was in the original cast of The History Boys by Alan Bennet.  Alongside his stage and screen work, he has appeared in numerous radio dramas.

Abridged by Katrin Williams
Produced by Elizabeth Allard
